title: "Optimization"
subtitle: "Differentiable design — tuning a foraging colony end-to-end"

And because a Plexus design is just a **spec** — a handful of numbers over a fixed operator
set — that design can be *optimized*, not only simulated. The forager here is a colony of
**deformable cells**: each cell is a soft elastic body simulated with **MPM** (the
material-point method), and the colony navigates by **chemotaxis** — sensing an attractant
gradient that points toward the food and climbing it — coordinated by boids flocking, with
MPM handling the physical push against walls and neighbours. A black-box **UCB** search tunes
the spec's parameters — motility speed and turn rate, sensing gain, material stiffness
(`youngs`), cell size and count, and the four boids weights — from a hand-set design (left) to
the best found (right), which delivers food roughly **five-fold faster**.

## Harder navigation

The same recipe scales to harder navigation — a porous **pillar** field and a walled **maze**,
each crossed by climbing a food-attractant gradient that itself flows around the obstacles, and
tuned by the same optimizer. Each strip runs left → right, from its starting point to the
optimized colony.

**Pillars — a porous field**

{{< video gallery/race_pillars_winner_1.mp4 title="pillars — starting point" >}}

{{< video gallery/race_pillars_winner_8.mp4 title="pillars — optimized (136/154 escape the porous field)" >}}

**Maze — a walled labyrinth**

{{< video gallery/race_maze_hard_winner_1.mp4 title="maze — starting point" >}}

{{< video gallery/race_maze_hard_winner_5.mp4 title="maze — optimized (150/160 solve the labyrinth)" >}}

The colony never “sees” the maze — it only reads a local food-attractant gradient — yet the
optimizer discovers spec parameters that route the population through the labyrinth. Same
operators, same engine; only the spec changed.
